utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: Good morning. Would you be seated, please, and have the accused brought in? (The accused entered court)

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: I would like to say good morning to everybody. I hope that everybody hears me, the interpreters, good morning. All right, we can begin. Mr. Kehoe, will you be conducting the examination-in-chief?

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. President, and I will be here with my colleague, Mr. van der Does. It's basically a solo flight with just the two of us, so that's all who will be here today. Maybe Mr. Cayley will be joining us later.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: You know, you got a strong back. You can do it all by yourself. I'm sure you can do it all by yourself. All right, go ahead.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: The next witness is a witness, the pseudonym for this witness will we be Witness WW. If I could go into either private or closed session while I go into some of my preliminary remarks, some of those remarks will be of an identifying nature, and if we can do those in closed session. We have consulted with counsel on this so I don't believe there's any objection in that regard.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: The registrar said that we can now have private session in here.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Yes, that's correct. We can move into a private session.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: Will that be all right, private session?

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: That's perfectly okay, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: Any problems with the Defence? Mr. Kehoe, go ahead. (Private session).

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: (Open session)

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: I would ask Mr. Dubuisson, and with the assistance of the usher, if we could take this particular exhibit with the circles on it and have that put on the ELMO and handed out to counsel and Your Honours, I think it would be helpful.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: This will be 402.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, Witness WW, you have seen this exhibit 402 previously; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And you assisted me to make these various marks on this map of the village of Svinjarevo; is that right?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, using the map that is on the ELMO before you, Exhibit 402, can you explain to the Judges what happened beginning on the morning of the 18th of April, 1993?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: On the 18th of April, 1993 in the morning at 6.30 a.m., the Croatian Defence Council attacked the village of Svinjarevo. First, there was intense shelling from the village of Hadrovci, this is the area, and the village of Brezova Kosa, to the right of the main Busovaca-Kiseljak road.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Those are the areas that you're marking as letters "A" and "B"; is that right?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, these two villages here. (Indicating).

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: No, the particular shelling areas, sir, the areas of the shelling?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: It's called Purisevo. It was shelled from Hadrovci and Brezova Kosa.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Just continue with your story, sir.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: After the shelling, the HVO soldiers started to go along the ridge from Hadrovci towards the village of Purisevo and the hamlet of Purovo. As soon as the infantry entered the village, they burned the ten houses that were in that first hamlet, and then they went on to the second village, Japojrevo. There, they captured three civilians. We still don't know where they had been buried, and they had not been exchanged. They were captured on the 18th as civilians. Also on the 18th, I left the village of Svinjarevo, I left this inhabited area next to the main Busovaca-Kiseljak road. We left along this route and went to the village of Mahala and we set up a front-line there along this village here next to this cemetery here to the left. On the 18th, we set up the line here, and the Croats remained in this area. And this was the situation that lasted a whole day. The demarcation between the HVO and the TO, that area, the no-man's land, was about 100 metres. On that same day, the 18th of April, when this line was set up and the purpose of that was to evacuate the civilian population from this area down there, I went back along the same route that we used to retreat into this inhabited area. And in the early evening, the civilian population remained in their houses.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Let me stop you there for one moment, Witness WW, and if we could put this second exhibit on the ELMO, Exhibit 403. Now, Witness WW, we are discussing, with Exhibit 403, the evening of the 18th of April, 1993. Could you tell the Judges what you did during that time frame with the civilians using Exhibit 403 as a guide?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: On the 18th of April, 1993 in the evening hours, we evacuated the civilian population from the lower part of Svinjarevo. And this area Rausevac, we had four Muslim houses there, and they went to this inhabited area on that same day, the inhabited area of Svinjarevo. In the dusk hours just before the nightfall, we left with the civilians along this route here, 200 civilians, and we arrived to the village of Mahala. We immediately went on along this route and along the ridge to the location of Medinik, and the civilians went into the municipality of Visoko.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: There's an arrow at the top of the circle which comes from just below that which is part of Jehovac. Did some other villagers move up and meet you in the Mahala and also be evacuated? Where are you pointing?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: On that same day, that's the 18th of April, the village of Jehovac, the inhabitants, about 40 of them from this area right here, you can see it quite clear, they were also evacuated on the 18th into this village. And then along the same route, they left together with the other inhabitants to the municipality of Visoko.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: How many civilians did you evacuate on the evening of the 18th of April, 1993?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: On the 18th of April, we evacuated around 220 civilians.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: With the assistance of the usher, if we could now move back to Exhibit 402, the previous exhibit. Now, you noted that in the morning hours, the HVO burnt the villages that are designated in letters "D" and "E"?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And that thereafter, that evening, you evacuated the civilian population on the evening of the 18th of April?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Tell the Judges what happened after that.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: After that, on the 19th of April, I went back at 10.00 a.m. with two or three other men, soldiers of the TO, we went back along the same route which was used by the civilian population to leave the village of Svinjarevo to the village of Mahala. We went back to Svinjarevo, right there at the middle of this road here, and we remained there until noon. Then around noon, these four houses in the village of Rausevac were set on fire. This is predominantly a Croatian village. Around 2.00, the HVO soldiers from the village of Rausovic came here to the main road in Svinjarevo and stole two cars. This is the middle of the street. They took those cars out of garages and drove them away to the main Busovaca-Kiseljak route. Then they burned about ten houses from this garage here, where the cars were stolen, all the way down to the bridge, that's where the river flows through the village. And then those civilians who remained, about 18 of them who did not leave on the 18th, because they probably thought that the conflict would cease, that this was just a temporary thing, they stayed in their houses here in this part and also on the right bank of the river. However, the HVO soldiers captured the civilians and took them to the Kiseljak barracks. On the 19th, four civilians of those 19 who remained in Jehovac were killed, so they were killed on the 19th by HVO soldiers. The remaining civilians who had been taken to the Kiseljak barracks were detained there for two or three days. And then three days later, they were taken back to three Muslim houses, Bosniak houses, in Jehovac along the main route. And Croats live there nowadays because the houses still stand. When they were returned from the Kiseljak barracks to Jehovac, they were all exchanged through their neighbours, Croats, who drove them in their cars to Visoko where they were exchanged. Only two remained out of that group. They lived in a Bosniak house here, the middle one of those three houses here, until July 1993. In the evening around 10.00 p.m., a neighbour from Jehovac came and drove them away. I don't know how much time passed after that, but the remains of two of them were brought to Visoko and were handed over and buried.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So the burning that took place on the 19th took place in the area designated on the map as "F" and the area designated on the map around the letter "G"; is that right?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Continue, sir.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: On the 20th of April, '93, the demarcation line was at the village of Mahala. And here up around the cemetery, there was shelling, not so much shelling, on the side of HVO and shooting, infantry shooting. On the 21st, the HVO soldiers arrived from Svinjarevo, and they came along these woods to the lines of TO here around this village Mahala. And the civilians had left that village on the 18th. This was probably just a reconnaissance, and we started shooting, and they went back again. The reconnaissance came back this way to the beginning of the village of Svinjarevo, this part here, up to here. About twenty houses were burned on the 21st in Spahinje, this little hamlet here. This was burnt down as well. There were no civilians there. There were seven to eight houses there. But on the 23rd, there was a big action prepared and the shelling continued. The HVO committed this shelling from Hadrovci, Rausevac, Brezova Kosa and Podastinje which is close to Kiseljak. There was heavy shelling from mortar and very heavy attack. And we left the lines around 2.00 in the afternoon, so we left them completely, this village here and this part here around the cemetery, and we drove to this part here, Stojkovici, Medenik. On the 23rd, after this heavy shelling, we went out into this part here, and I was seriously injured and five other members of TO. We were taken later on to the hospital in Visoko. I don't know what happened further during the following months, but I only know that within one month, all of this region fell, and the Croatians took over this part. During the fall of this hamlet, Mahala, this village Mahala where about ten families lived, was completely burned down. This part down here where I couldn't see properly up there, because we were already moved from this village up to there, I could see this part here from this part here. What you have evidence on the maps and on the photographs from the 200 facilities here, only one house remained untouched. That means that all the other houses were destroyed and burned down. Only one house remained where the Croats lived from all these facilities there.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, Witness WW, let me ask you a couple of questions about this map. When this attack was taking place in Svinjarevo, were other villages around Svinjarevo also being attacked by the HVO?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: At the same moment on the 18th of April, the village Behrec and Gomionica were attacked.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, you noted that there were houses burnt on the 18th on the two areas circled "D" and "E"; is that right?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You also noted on the 19th that houses were burnt on the map in the areas circled "F" and "G"?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: On the 19th in the areas "F" and "G," was there any TO resistance in that area?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No, there was no resistance on the side of TO, because on the 18th of April when the attack began, we came from the lower part to this village Mahala, so that we could, on the 18th in the evening, take these 220 civilians outside and to give them some security. Because there were still some area free, about some 100 metres free, from HVO. If the HVO soldiers had taken these 100 metres, all these civilians would have no way out, and they would have to remain down here.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, you also noted that on the 21st of April, the areas circled on the map "I" and "H" were burnt by HVO forces; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Was there any Territorial Defence resistance in those areas when those houses were burnt by the HVO?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No, there was no resistance. On the 21st, this village, there was nobody, no civilians, no members of the TO, especially this part down here that already belonged -- that was part of the main road. There were no members of the TO.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: On the 23rd, there are three areas circled, "J," "K" and "L." Was there TO resistance in those areas when they were burnt by the HVO?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No, there was no resistance because there were no civilians and no members of the TO. Because already on the 23rd, the civilians that remained in this area were already taken care of in these three houses here that are on the main road, Busovaca-Kiseljak, in a Bosniak house here in the middle. So no civilians were moving around these areas.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did you see on the 23rd smoke emanating from these -- coming from these homes circled "L" and "K"?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I could see smoke from this lower part and from this part here. So houses were burning and we could see the smoke when we were standing on this hill here, Stojkovici.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: The area that you're pointing to as Stojkovici is the area that is designated "M" at the top of the map; is that right?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, yes, yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, you were wounded on the 23rd, is that correct, and taken to the hospital in Visoko?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: How many structures would destroyed during that time frame? How many structures belonging to Bosnian Muslims were destroyed?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: From the 23rd on or you mean all together?

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: From the 18th to the 23rd, approximately, during that time frame when the HVO attacked?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Around 100 structures.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Was cattle taken as well or destroyed?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, they were taking away some cattle, and there was a lot of cattle that burned down together with the structures.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You mentioned previously on the 19th, there was the theft of several automobiles on the road back towards Kiseljak; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, that's right. When the soldiers came on the 19th of April, '93, and they entered half of the village of Jehovac, they took -- because there were some better, more luxurious cars, they took those cars and these other cars that remained, they burnt down as well. They didn't take them but they were burnt down at the place where they were.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Witness WW, how many civilians were killed during this conflict in April of 1993?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: In Svinjarevo, there were 10 civilians killed. Where eight of them are, we still don't know. And for these two, we know because they were exchanged in Visoko.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Were any civilians taken captive during this time period?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, these that were taken to Kiseljak, they spent some time at the barracks in Kiseljak, and they were returned to this house here at the main road where you see that there are three houses.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Were any of those civilians that were taken captive, were they killed during the time when they were being held captive?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, these two were killed that I have already spoken about that were exchanged in Visoko. And the eight, together with these two, ten, they were exchanged. The neighbours, depending on who knew whom, took them to Visoko and then they exchanged them depending on certain relations or acquaintances.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: If we can move to the next exhibit, Mr. President, Your Honours and Mr. Dubuisson, which is this particular exhibit with the legend attached, which will be 404 and 404A, I believe?

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: That's correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Mr. President, if we can ask the legend be placed under seal because it does identify the house belonging to Witness WW.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: We have to be careful here because, if I've understood correctly, the photographs can be seen in the public gallery, that is, the maps.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Yes, that's correct, if we put them on the ELMO, then we're going to have to go into closed session.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: Well, then we better have a closed session.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Mr. President, it's okay. I am simply going to ask the witness whether or not the legend accurately depicts the locations that are circled, and we need not go into the legend and we can just make that part of the record. So we're not going to go through the number of structures that were destroyed.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: We're not going to have the witness mention all 85 references. There would be no point in that. You can simply ask him if he can identify them in the way he marked them in the Office of the Prosecutor. If there's any challenge from the Defence, we'll deal with that as a separate issue. Let's try to simplify things. Mr. Kehoe, proceed, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President, if we can just put the map on the ELMO.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Witness WW, these are the structures that you circled that had been destroyed in part or in toto during the April time frame; is that right?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: The legend of names before you is the list of names where you described the individuals who owned these houses; is that right?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Other than the number 29, which is circled in orange, were all these structures that were destroyed, were they owned by Bosnian Muslims?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, structure 29, that was a structure that was owned by a Bosnian Croat; is that right?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, which still is.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: There was a structure that was owned by a Bosnian Muslim that is on the map circled as 28 which was also not destroyed; is that right?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, that's right. There are still Croatians living there.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: The family that owned structure 29, did they move their relatives into that house that was not destroyed, number 28?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Thank you very much. We can move on. The last exhibit that I would like to address, Mr. President, as briefly as possible is a series of photographs that I mentioned during my prefatory remarks which is a sampling of some of the structures that were destroyed in the village of Svinjarevo during this April time frame. At this point, I would ask that we go into a private session, because there are various photographs at the various angles of Witness WW's house.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: All right. Then we will go into a private session. (Private session)

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: (Open session)

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: While we're discussing this unit, is the name of the unit at least correct?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: The name of the unit is correct because all the villages are taken by that. It is not true that these are all soldiers from Svinjarevo. These are villages that belonged from Svinjarevo to Gomionica.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Is it true that this unit was a part of the BiH army?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: It couldn't be together and it couldn't be tied to it, and we never left the village and went to the frontlines. If we had gone to the front-line at that time, then it would have been a unit of the BiH army.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: According to this document, were you a part of the BiH army or not?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: TO, we were TO, because in '92, there was no fighting between the Croats and the Bosniaks, and the BiH army could not have acted at the municipality of Kiseljak at that time.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Then why does the commander of BiH army appoint you if you were not part of the BiH army?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: He appointed me only when I left the police, '93, '92 in August. It was not BiH army but TO, we could say that, in the village.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: How is it that the commander of a company of the BiH army appoints you as the commander if you are not a part of the BiH army?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: At that time, there was no BiH army. Maybe sometime in '93, there was a BiH army formed. At this area of Kiseljak, there was no BiH army.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: But you were the BiH army?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No, we were not because we didn't fight.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: But according to this document, you were BiH army?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Maybe according to you.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Well, these soldiers, the Territorial Defence, whatever you want to call them, did they live in their houses in the village?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, until the fighting started on the 18th.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did they eat in their houses?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Until the fighting of the 18th, yes, of course, they lived with their families. Each of them lived in his or her house.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: The weapons and the ammunition that you had, did you keep them in your homes?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No, we knew exactly how many weapons we had and where we had these weapons and where the guards were. Nobody kept the weapons in the house.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did you patrol the village?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, normally, because together in '92, we did the same thing with the Croats together from Rausevic.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did you dig trenches and build bunkers above the village?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No, there were maybe a few places, but we were digging them together in '92. Croats and Bosniaks were digging the lines towards Visoko. When Visoko started fighting with Serbs, we were digging together until '92, until the division occurred. When the Croats separated, they didn't want to continue with us. They separated to their villages and we went to ours, and that was what the situation was like from '92 to '93.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: What about bunkers?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: Witness WW, if you don't mind, when you answer the questions, would you look at the Judges, please? Thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Were there any bunkers further up from the village?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No, there were no bunkers.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: The area of the responsibility of the unit under your command, was it Medjumostine, Svinjarevo, Purisevici (phoen), Mahavici (phoen)?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Normally. That was that zone that existed, but we didn't really have lines. We weren't dug in.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Was that your area of responsibility?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No, that was not a zone. This was only where the Bosniaks were. It was normal that in the evening we had patrols, the same as the Croats did around their villages.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You testified that 10 civilians were killed all together. Do you know under which circumstances these civilians died? Did you see how, in what manner, each of them were killed?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I know that none of them had a gun in his hand, of these ten that died.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did you see the circumstances in which those people were killed, in what manner?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: The first three on the 18th that were captured were captured in Purisevo. So during the attack on the 18th, they were captured as civilians. Normally, in civilian structures, and I didn't see what happened -- to this day, they haven't been exchanged. One of them was 65 years of age.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Can you please give me a direct answer? Under which circumstances were those civilians killed?

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Excuse me, counsel. I would ask that counsel ask questions and not editorialise on whether or not he agrees or disagrees with his answer by commenting, "Please give me a direct answer."

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: Okay, objection sustained. Ask your questions, Mr. Nobilo, and let's move on. Continue, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. NOBILO
utterances.text: Mr. President, I was not commenting, but the witness is avoiding answering the question. I asked twice, and I attempted the third time. Please allow me to ask whether he knows under which circumstances these civilians were killed, and that's the only answer I want. I'm not commenting. Whether he knows, under which circumstances they were killed, that's a relevant question.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: On the 18th of April --

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: He's editorialising. Editorialising goes on often in the questions which I let go, and I don't object to it. The question that started off questioning why he doesn't answer his direct question, that is editorialising by counsel. And I simply ask counsel to ask questions and restrict his comments until final argument. That's all.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: Mr. Kehoe, let me say to you, there's always some degree of editorialising in questions. What I'm trying to do is to be sure that we respect certain limits. I've sustained your objection by telling Mr. Nobilo to avoid anything that might be comments. Now he has to ask questions as he wishes to. He is the Defence counsel, and he can ask questions as he likes. Have faith in me. I will be very attentive about all of this.

utterances.speaker: MR. NOBILO
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Witness WW, do you know under which circumstances those ten civilians were killed, any of them or all of them?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I don't know for all of them under which circumstances. I know that they were killed as civilians. On the 18th of April, these first three that were captured during the first day were captured in the first village that was burned down on the 18th. They were captured then. I don't know for how long they remained there. I don't know what exactly happened. We still don't know nowadays what happened to them. I know for these other civilians that were captured there normally, they saw the others that were killed, that they were killed in front of their houses or on some meadows while they were withdrawing, when they wanted to leave. I couldn't see everything, how each of them was killed. They saw them, for example, that they were killed while they were leaving or coming back.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Let's clarify this for the transcript. Can we then conclude that you know that they were killed but you don't know in what manner because you did not see it?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I know that they were killed, but I don't know in which way they were killed.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: Move to another question, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. NOBILO
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I would just like the names of those ten civilians to be mentioned?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Halilbasic Rifet, Colakovic Osman, Cutura Adem, Japaur Hamdo, Japaur Munever, Rahmanovic Mustafa, Osmanovic Enver, Mustajbegovic Halid, Japaur Ismet ...

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: All right, if you can't recall any more names. My next question is: Can we find any or all of these civilians on the list that I showed you a couple of minutes ago?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: You can find them, but at that time, these people all remained down there in the street. So they were not with the TO, so they didn't have a gun in their hand.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: How long did the resistance last?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: Mr. Nobilo, excuse me for interrupting you. I think this is almost the break time, so I want to know whether you still have a lot of questions to ask. It's just having to do with scheduling our hearing.

utterances.speaker: MR. NOBILO
utterances.text: Not a long time, but maybe it would be a good idea to have the break now. Ten minutes, fifteen minutes, it's hard to say.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: All right. We will take a 20-minute break. The court is adjourned.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: The hearing will resume now. Have the accused brought in, please. (The accused entered court)

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: Mr. Nobilo.

utterances.speaker: MR. NOBILO
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So we stopped at the time when we were trying to determine what's your idea, how long did this resistance last until you retreated from the municipality of Kiseljak?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: It lasted till I was wounded, so we were at the territory of Svinjarevo for five days.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: After you were wounded, did the unit remain there at the territory of the Kiseljak municipality?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, it remained there for another month.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: It's only the 25 people that you mentioned at the beginning that fought?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Normally, where I was.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Were there any soldiers killed in Svinjarevo?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: In Svinjarevo, no.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Not a single soldier, only ten civilians. Can you please tell me, do you know whether any houses were razed to the ground or burnt during that month and a half and five days when the fighting was more intense and closer to Svinjarevo? Were any houses damaged during the combat and due to the combat?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: The houses were destroyed mostly during the attack from burning, normally, not from the shells. None from the shells.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Your brother was killed.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Was he a soldier or a civilian?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: He was in the TO, member of the TO.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: He was killed in the fight around Svinjarevo; is that what you were telling us about?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, that's true, in the village Mahala. He was carrying food.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You said a little while ago that no soldiers were killed, only civilians. How do you explain that?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: He was carrying food.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: Stay within the scope of the examination-in-chief, please, Mr. Nobilo.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Behrec and Gomionica, you said these villages were attacked. Did they have their own units of the Territorial Defence or the BiH army?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Normally, they had. Each village had the TO.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Can we then say that the principal organisation of the Territorial Defence and the HVO in Bosnia was one village, one unit or several smaller villages, one unit? Can we say that this was the principle in both sides?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I don't know what the principle was like for HVO. I know that each village had their guards, at least the Bosniak villages, in '92.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You said that in this area there were 200 houses that were destroyed by one and that you evacuated 220 civilians through the woods. What about the rest of the population? When did they evacuate?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: All the destroyed villages that were in the upper part of Svinjarevo, for example, ten to fifteen houses, these were empty houses that the people had built and then they moved to new houses in Svinjarevo. So that these other ones were empty.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You meant abandoned?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, abandoned because people built new houses and they moved to these new houses before the fighting.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: But if 200 houses, less ten or fifteen, it's 180 or 185, and we have 220 civilians that you evacuated, so I ask you whether some inhabitants left the area before the fighting?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No, not ten to fifteen, there were four hamlets there, Purisevo, Mahala, and these were hamlets. This is not ten to fifteen houses, this is 50 or 60 houses.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So 60 abandoned old houses?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Approximately.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: We saw the pictures of your village. Can you please tell us, do you know when these photographs were taken?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No, I can't.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Were you in the village after it had been burnt down, after everything was finished in 1993?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No, I wasn't there in 1993, but when Dayton was signed, I went to the village Svinjarevo.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So you saw your village for the first time after the evacuation and the retreat in 1994, in February?

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: In 1993, you left the village?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, but during the Dayton Agreement --

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And when was the Dayton Agreement signed?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Somewhere in 1994.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So you can only testify as to the way that the village looked in 1994; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: '95. It was 1995 when I entered the village for the first time. It wasn't '94.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So you can only testify about the way that the village looked in 1995?

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: The villagers of your village, you are the chairman of the committee, I don't know what the official name is, of the agency for the return and the reconstruction of Svinjarevo, you're working on it, you're trying to rebuild the village, and you're planning to go back. But in the meantime, where did the people from your village live, those people who fled, the 220 people who fled?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Fojnica, Visoko, Kakanj, and Bilalovac.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Whose houses?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Mostly all of us live -- a very small number of us in Bosniak houses, a few of us in Serbian houses, and most of us in Croatian houses.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Let's go back to the very beginning when our client, Colonel Blaskic, came to Jehovac. What was the reason why he came there? Was it an official meeting or was it accidental?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No, there wasn't an official meeting. He just stopped by.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Can you tell us now from the distance and from your experience that you have now, among the villagers of Bosniak nationality, his arrival, his words, did it have a calming effect to the inter-ethnic relations?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes. Normally, it was calming us down and it worked because he told us that there would be no problems, that we should live together in that sense.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: This group in which you were when Colonel Blaskic arrived, was it only Bosniaks or were there also Croats there?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: There were four or five Bosniaks.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: The rest, were they Croats?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No, they were not Croats.

utterances.speaker: MR. NOBILO
utterances.text: So only Bosniaks. I have no further questions.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: Mr. Kehoe, do you want to ask any additional questions within the scope of the cross-examination?

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Of course. Just a couple of questions, and I would ask that Exhibit D142 that Defence counsel used with the witness be given to the witness? I'm sorry, 143. I apologise. Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Witness WW, how many weapons did the TO have to defend itself in the village of Svinjarevo on the morning of the 18th of April, 1993?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: We had about 25 rifles.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Now, what type of rifles were these?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Seven hunting rifles, eight M-48 rifles, ten rifles were automatic rifles.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Now, you were shelled that morning, were you not?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: What were you shelled with?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Sixty-millimetre mortars, 80-millimetre mortars, 120-millimetre mortars, and also one or two anti-aircraft guns.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Did you have any mortars or any anti-aircraft weapons to respond to the shelling by the HVO?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Now let's turn to this Exhibit D143 that Defence counsel gave you. Do you see that before you?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Now, is this the list of every living male up to approximately 50-something, I suppose, living in the Svinjarevo-Behrici-Rudnik area?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Let's look at this first page. Do you know a man by the name of Rahamovic Nezir?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Did he ever participate in any of the TO activities?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No, he didn't even participate in the guard duty.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: What about Kebic Mirsad, the next individual?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Look down that page. Do you know a man by the name of Purisevic Nurija?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: Could you indicate the pages, please? I'm not following you very clearly. I've got the first -- the first one -- we're on what page?

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: These aren't paged; Defence counsel hasn't paginated them. It's a page that has Bego Seid as the first name, Judge. All I'm going through is a list of these people; a lot of these people never participated in any of this. There's no pages on this, Judge, which is a little difficult. It says Command III --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: Maybe it's page 5. There's a number 5 on the top. Is it page 5 then? All the way on the top. That's what my colleagues are pointing out to me. Is that it?

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: I think so, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RIAD
utterances.text: Yes, we found it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: All right. Thank you to my colleagues. Continue, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Do you know someone by the name of Purisevic Nurija?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: What was his physical condition at that time?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Well, bad. He was 80 per cent disabled.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: So at the time of the war, he's 80 per cent disabled.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Did he fight with you during these attack periods of time in 1993?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Let's continue down that page. Do you know a man by the name of Japaur Asef?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: What was his physical condition?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Well, it was bad. He was not with us at all.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Continue down that page. Rahmanovic Husein. Do you know that man?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: What was his physical condition?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Bad. He had been in a traffic accident.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Let's turn to the next page, which is the page, Your Honour, which has I VOD and then the Roman numeral II. Let's go down, in that first group, let's look at Ibreljic Vahid. Do you know that man?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Did he participate with you?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: What was the matter with him?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: He had a spine condition.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Let's continue down to the next group. Brkanovic Hasan. Do you know that man?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Did he ever participate?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: What about the next group, Behlil Ramiz. Where was he from?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: He was from the village of Rudnik.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Did he ever participate?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No, because he was in Kiseljak, and he baked bread with Hrvoje in the municipality of Kiseljak during the conflict.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RIAD
utterances.text: Excuse me. What do you mean by "participate"?

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: A lot of these people on here never were involved in the TO, never did anything. This is a group or list that is simply on paper, Judge, and it's not a reality as to what was happening. What has happened is these lists were developed before that were obviously taken and it's a list of every living man there that didn't actually do anything, that didn't fight.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RIAD
utterances.text: Were they participating in fighting or in ensuring the security of a village? I mean, there are many participations.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: They didn't do anything.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RIAD
utterances.text: Could you just be clear?

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: The individuals that we talked about so far, Witness WW, did they participate in any way in guarding or defending the village?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Continue on that same list. Behlil Mujo, do you know that individual?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Did he participate in defending or guarding the village?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Let's continue on with the next name, Hodurda, and pardon my pronunciation, Bajazid. Do you see that name?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Did he participate?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Continue on that list. Keep going down. Behlil Hasan, did he participate?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: So, Witness WW, based on your experience with the TO in Svinjarevo, does this list of people made in '92 accurately depict who was working in the TO when the HVO attacked on the 18th of April, 1993?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I did not understand your question.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Is this an accurate list of the members of the TO as of April 18th, 1993? Is this a list on paper or is this actually the amount of soldiers you had?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: This is just a theoretical list.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Now, you were asked by Defence counsel, when you went back into the village, and you said you went back into the village after the Dayton Peace Accords; is that right?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: When you were in the village in April of 1993, did you see the HVO burning all of these houses while you were at various locations, and did you see smoke emanating from other locations where it clearly indicated that they were burning those houses?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Was there any military reason for them to burn every house in Svinjarevo?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No military reason because all the houses that were burnt in the lower part, there were no members of the Territorial Defence.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: In fact, sir, did you see HVO soldiers pouring petrol or benzene on houses to burn them on occasion?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I saw on the 23rd, in the village of Mahala, that was when Mahala fell, the last house was burned in the following way: A lad that was burning the houses carried a jerrycan. That's the only thing I saw. I didn't see how they set the fire to other buildings.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: And after you saw him carrying the jerrycan, did the houses go up in flames?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: All the houses before were already in flames bar that last one, and that last one, the last house in the village, was also set on fire. I saw the soldier carry a jerrycan, he entered the house, and all of a sudden, there was this smoke and flames coming from the inside.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Mr. President, Your Honours, I have no further questions. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: Thank you. The Judges are going to ask some questions now.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RIAD
utterances.text: Good morning, Witness WW. I just would like to understand more clearly a few things.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RIAD
utterances.text: What do you mean by, this was a theoretical list, about the list, if I understand you? What do you mean by it was a theoretical list?

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Excuse me. This is a public hearing --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: Yes. In respect of the words that are being said, I would like to remind you that this is now a public hearing, so in respect of the questions that you want to ask, Judge Riad, would you prefer that we have a private session? That might be better. All right. We're going to move into a private session. (Private session)

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: (Open session)

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: We're back in public session now, are we? Mr. Kehoe, it's now 25 after 12. Do you have any other witnesses? Would you prefer us to wait until the afternoon? Where are we?

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: I would prefer, Mr. President, if we could wait until the afternoon with the court's permission.

utterances.speaker: MR. NOBILO
utterances.text: Mr. President, if we may suggest, we agree, but these 35 minutes, that goes the time of the Prosecutor.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYMAN
utterances.text: I have a different request. I would ask the court to instruct the Prosecutor not to discuss this list with the next witness who, I think, is also from the (redacted). Let's get the witness's own impressions of the list without the extra two hours of preparation concerning this list if, indeed, the next witness is from (redacted). So we would ask for a sequestering of the next witness on that limited issue from the Prosecution during the lunch break.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: Now you're empowering me with powers more greater than those given to me by the statute, and I don't know what I can answer. Mr. Kehoe, were you planning to prepare the next witness? Did you plan to have lunch with the next witness and to prepare him again?

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Your Honour, I don't know what counsel is afraid of. Have no fear. I will not have lunch with the next witness. I will not sit down and chat with the next witness and maybe go to the beach together. I mean, I don't know what the import is of counsel's arguments. Have no fear, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: Anyway, we don't have enough time. Very well, I think that's the end of this incident. However, Mr. Nobilo asked that the 35 minutes be counted as part of the Prosecution case. You know that I'm trying to apply this rule as flexibly as I can, but it's true that there are a lot of holes in our schedule. Therefore, it is legitimate that this be counted as part of the Prosecution's time. Now let me turn to my colleagues. Very well, the Judges say that we will resume at a quarter after two, 2.15.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. President. --- Luncheon recess taken at 12.27 p.m. 20 21 22 23 24 25

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: (Open session)

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: We will resume the hearing now. Have the accused brought in, please? (The accused entered court)

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: We can resume now. Mr. Cayley, you are going to represent the Prosecution; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: Good afternoon, Mr. President, Your Honours, Counsel. Yes, I am. The Prosecutor now proposes to adduce additional evidence in support of paragraphs 5 and 5.1, these being part of the general allegations in the second amended indictment against General Blaskic. I think it is now accepted jurisprudence within this Tribunal that in order for those charges, which are grave breaches and which rely upon the Geneva Convention for their legal foundation, the four Geneva Conventions, there must be a preliminary finding by the court under paragraph 5 and 5.1. It is this finding which, if you will, triggers the grave breaches provisions of the Geneva Conventions. Now, the requirements of that finding and its factual parameters are a matter for closing argument between the parties and, ultimately, judicial finding. Now is not the appropriate time for that argument. However, I think it would not be improper or ill-founded of me at this time to say that, broadly speaking, this part of the proof concerns the extent and manner of the military and political relationship between the Republic of Croatia and the HV on the one side, and the Croatian community, later Republic of Herceg-Bosna, and the HVO on the other side. To this is logically connected the role and involvement of the Republic of Croatia in the affairs of the Republic of Bosnia-Herzegovina from 1991 to 1994. At the outset, I would like to submit to the Chamber and to the Defence two tabulated dossiers containing a number of documents. Mr. Registrar, if those documents could be distributed to the court? These documents, along with oral testimony and a few other documents which we will submit towards the end of the case, are our proofs for this part of the case. There will be no oral testimony for this part of the proceedings. How I propose to proceed, Mr. President, if you're in agreement, is to, in essence, give a summary of these documents. Within that summary, I hope to highlight the evolution of these assembled papers, relying exclusively on the facts contained within the documents. I will not be drawing any conclusion, giving any argument at all. That is not for this part of the case. There are 113 documents in these two dossiers. I intend to go through some of the documents individually, but with others, I simply propose to speak about groups of documents. The index provided to all of the parties indicates the origin of each individual document.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYMAN
utterances.text: May I, Counsel?

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: Please.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYMAN
utterances.text: Mr. President, we are not sure what this procedure is. We are unaware of it and have not had any prior information about it. If the Prosecution has documents they wish to offer, we certainly find that appropriate. We can look at them. We may not have objection to any of them. We may have objection to some of them, and we can respond in due course. But counsel is not a witness. He's not a summary witness. He's not a fact witness. He's not a legal expert witness. He's no kind of witness. And this is -- nor is this time for closing argument or the time for a summary of other evidence. We're entirely unfamiliar with the type of proceeding that counsel is proposing. We've listened. We will listen further about exactly what the nature of this proceeding is and, perhaps, take guidance from the court, of course, ultimately. But as far as we know, in my system and the continental system that Mr. Nobilo is expert in, parties can offer documents, and then at the end of the case, comment on them, but parties don't comment on documents directly to the court in the middle of the case.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: I would like to deliberate with my colleagues.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: Mr. President, would it be appropriate for me to respond to the --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: Yes, excuse me. I forgot to give you the floor before I conferred with my colleagues. I'm referring to Rule 85, but we'll listen to you first, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: My learned friend has misinterpreted what I said or, perhaps, has misheard me. I'm not presenting myself as a witness. We are in a unique institution in this court. We are not obliged to follow the particular rules of any common law or civil law system. The rules provide that any evidence may be admitted by a Chamber if it is relevant and if it is deemed to have probative value. There are no requirements in the rules as to how that particular evidence can be presented. Indeed, Rule 85 speaks that each party is entitled to call witnesses and present evidence. There is no requirement that a witness needs to be called to present this particular evidence. As I've already stated earlier, I have no intention of making any sort of argument about these documents. My intent is simply to give a summary to the court, if you will, a navigational chart, so that the most important aspects of these documents can be highlighted to the court. We can identify the origin of all but one of these documents. The court can be secure in that fact. So I'm perfectly happy to argue later with my learned friend about the question of admissibility, which I think is, in my view and the Prosecutor's view, beyond doubt. These documents can be admitted into evidence, and there is nothing in the rules which precludes us from offering evidence in this manner.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYMAN
utterances.text: Those are two different questions, Mr. President, whether the documents --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: Mr. Hayman, I can give the floor back to you, but you had your response. All right, go ahead. Go ahead, but do it quickly, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYMAN
utterances.text: Just for clarity of the argument. There are two different issues. Documents may well be self-authenticating and we may not object to them, and documents can come in without a witness. That's one issue. A separate issue is whether counsel, in the middle of their case, can lecture the court on what documents contain and, perhaps, what they mean. We don't think the latter is appropriate. The former, we don't know if there is a dispute because we have never seen these binders before. And we would propose, quite frankly, the court can admit them subject to the Defence having the opportunity to review them and raise any objections or concerns we may. Then we proceed with the next witness.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: Thank you. The Judges decide that an application of Rule 85(A) of the rules, each of the parties is entitled to call and present evidence. We are in this case here, and the Judges, therefore, accept that the Prosecutor can present the evidence which is found in these documents. However, as regards admissibility, this could be discussed at the time when the Defence replies through the presentation of its own evidence. For the time being, we admit the presentation, by the Prosecutor, of the evidence. The admissibility, as well as the relevance, will be discussed and admitted by the Tribunal, of course, in light of any answers that the Defence may make at the proper time, and that may be at any time. We will, therefore, continue and we will hear what Mr. Cayley has to present us as evidence.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: If I can just reassure a concern that my learned friend has expressed. I am in no way going to draw any conclusions from these documents at that time. That would be improper of me. I simply intend to summarise, in a very short period of time, probably about 20 minutes, the broad content of these documents.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: Well, take as much as time as you need. We have taken a decision. We accept that this is presented. If you need more than 20 minutes, then take more than 20 minutes. Conciseness is not really part of the discussion here. Take the time that you need. That's your problem.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: Very well.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: A number of documents are confidential and we will have to move into closed session for those documents. They have been provided to the Tribunal on a confidential basis, but I will express at the time the necessity, with your permission, Mr. President, to move into private session. A number of the documents have been translated into the French language, not all of them. We will endeavour to have a full set of translations before the end of the case. If I can refer the court, first of all, to document 1. In July of 1991, the Bosnian branch of the Croatian Democratic Union or the HDZ --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: Are we in a closed session here?

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: For the time being, this is still public.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: You would prefer that this be completely closed, Mr. Cayley?

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: It can be open for the time being, Mr. President, and I will let you know at the appropriate time.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: Very well. All right then, for the time being, we will remain in public session.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: In July of 1991, the Bosnian branch of the HDZ, the Croatian Democratic Union, met in Busovaca. Present were leaders of the Bosnian HDZ from Kresevo, Kiseljak, Fojnica, Busovaca, Vitez, Novi Travnik and Travnik. Dario Kordic presided at that meeting. There was deep concern expressed about the security situation in Bosnia-Herzegovina and Croatia. A number of conclusions were reached, including that the Republic of Croatia was the victim of aggression at the hands of the JNA and the Chetniks, and that in Bosnia-Herzegovina, a silent occupation was being carried out by the Serbs. In light of that Serb threat to Bosnia-Herzegovina, a rallying call was made to all Croats in Bosnia-Herzegovina. A clear reference is made in this document to the protection of Croat interests in Bosnia-Herzegovina.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: Mr. Cayley, could you please slow down for the sake of the interpreters?

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: And a proposal is made within this document for the formation of the Croatian National Council to represent the authority for the Croat peoples in Bosnia-Herzegovina as an alternative to the Bosnian official authorities. The document makes clear reference to Croatia as the motherland and calls on the president of the Bosnian branch of the Croatian Democratic Union to arrange an urgent session of the HDZ, BiH main board on the 24th of July, 1991 and calls four leaders of the HDZ in Zagreb, in the Republic of Croatia, to attend that session. Document 2: This is a document of the 12th of November of 1991, and it sets out a policy of an organisation termed the Croatian Regional Community of Herzegovina and the Travnik Regional Community of Croats. That policy is declared as the formation of a common Croatian state formed from the Republic of Croatia and those areas as claimed as Croatian territories within Bosnia-Herzegovina. The document refers to previous agreements with the presence of Croatia in Zagreb, in this regard, on the 30th and 20th of June, 1991. Document 3 demonstrates that by March of 1992, large sums of money were being made available by the Republic of Croatia for the physical defence of Croat interests in Bosnia-Herzegovina. Document 4 shows that at the same time, the late Gojka Susak, then Minister of Defence for the Republic of Croatia, is called upon by the Central Bosnian command of Bosnian Croat forces for instruction for military action in the area of Central Bosnia. If we can move ahead now to document 5. On the 21st of March of 1992, Dr. Franjo Tudjman, the president of the Republic of Croatia, writes to Alija Izetbegovic, the President of the Republic of Bosnia, and by way of formal decision recognises the state of Bosnia-Herzegovina and offers citizenship to the Republic of Croatia, to members of the Croatian nation in Bosnia-Herzegovina. The next set of documents can be taken as a group, and they are documents 6 to 22. On the 10th of April of 1992, Dr. Tudjman appoints General Janko Bobetko in command of all units of the Croatian army, the HV, on the southern front from the cities of Split to Dubrovnik. A staff is ordered to be formed at the same time. Document 7 shows that on the 12th of April, 1992, an order is issued by the commander of the Split operative zone, Mate Viduka, on the order of General Bobetko, to move the 4th Brigade of the Croatian National Guard Corps to the defence of Citluk in Bosnia-Herzegovina. The brigade is ordered to remove all Croatian army insignia before proceeding to Citluk and to present themselves as volunteer defenders of the homeland.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Please slow down.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: I'm sorry.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RIAD
utterances.text: Perhaps you could repeat that?

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: Document 7, Judge Riad, is an order of the 12th of April, 1992, issued by the commander of the Split operative zone, a man by the name of Mate Viduka, on the order of General Bobetko, a Croatian lieutenant-general, to move the 4th Brigade of the Croatian National Guard Corps to the defence of Citluk, which is a town in Bosnia-Herzegovina. The brigade is ordered to remove all Croatian army insignia before proceeding to Citluk and to present themselves as volunteer defenders of the homeland. Document 8 is an order of General Bobetko of the 16th of April of 1992. This Croatian lieutenant-general establishes a forward command post of his southern command in Grude in Bosnia-Herzegovina. Document 8 has attached to it the seal of the main staff of Herceg-Bosna, and it appoints Colonel Milivoj Petkovic as the deputy of General Janko Bobetko, a Croatian lieutenant-general. Document 9. On the 19th of April of 1992, General Bobetko orders the preparation of the defence of Livno and Tomislavgrad, both of these places being 20 kilometres inside the national border of Bosnia-Herzegovina. Again, this order is signed by General Bobetko as commander of the Croatian southern front and is sealed "Herceg-Bosna Main Staff." Document 10. On the 20th of April of 1992, General Bobetko, Croatian lieutenant-general, appoints a number of officers of the HVO of the Croatian community of Herceg-Bosna. He still signs, from the Grude command post, as commander of the southern front, but this time you will note from the document that his orders are given on the headed paper of the Croatian community of Herceg-Bosna, Croatian Defence Council. Document 11. On the same day, General Bobetko appoints Major General Ante Roso and Brigadier Miljenko Crnjec to command positions in the HVO. One is placed in command of Livno and the other in charge of the Duvno-Prozor-Konjic region. Both Prozor and Konjic are at least 60 kilometres inside Bosnia-Herzegovina from its border with the Republic of Croatia. Document 12, again on that day, the 21st of April, General Bobetko calls Major General Ante Roso, General Slobodan Praljak and Brigadier Crnjec to report to him for a briefing. Again, this is on the headed notepaper of the HVO and the HZ-HB, the Croatian community of Herceg-Bosna. Document 13 is a document of the 4th of May, 1992, where, as commander of the southern front command of the army of the Republic of Croatia, General Bobetko transmits an order from the main staff of the Croatian army to the headquarters of the HVO in respect of military training requirements. Now, a document which may seem out of place and interrupts the continuity of these documents is Resolution 752, which is document 14, Resolution 752 of the Security Council, and this is a document that demands that both the army of the Republic of Croatia and the JNA cease from interfering in Bosnia-Herzegovina, withdraw, and respect the territorial integrity of the country, and that document is dated the 15th of May and is provided in English and French. Move on now to document 15. On the 16th of May, 1992, one day after Resolution 752 is passed by the Security Council, General Bobetko issues orders to Major General Roso to strengthen his position in Tomislavgrad, a town in Bosnia-Herzegovina; he moves Colonel Milivoj Petkovic to Tomislavgrad and notifies General Roso that he is requesting the Minister of Defence of Croatia to visit the town of Tomislavgrad to use his authority to eliminate all groups and individuals who claim to act on the Croatian Minister's authority. Document 16 --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: You're going a little quickly there. I'm trying to follow you in English at the same time. This is the fifth member -- what is the last part you say there? Will be replaced what?

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: This is document 15, Mr. President, and if you note in paragraph 5 --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: All right. I see. All right. Fine.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: The General, General Janko Bobetko, is notified --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: I don't go quite as quickly as you do when it comes to reading English. Excuse me. I'm trying to follow what you're doing and to get to the essentials. It's all right. I see where you are. Go ahead, go ahead. Yes, okay. I wanted to learn English so badly that I didn't even look at the French text. Thank you very much. Go ahead. Go to 17. All right.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: Moving ahead now to document 16. On the 19th of May of 1992, and this document is in French, General Bobetko, as commander of the southern front command of the Croatian army, establishes a forward command post for Central Bosnia covering the municipalities of Busovaca, Vitez, Novi Travnik, Travnik, Bugonjo, Gornji Vakuf, Prozor, Tomislavgrad and Posusje, and appoints Brigadier Zarko Tole as commander of the IZM Central Bosnia. Document 17. On the 10th of June of 1992, Gojko Susak, the Minister of Defence of the Republic of Croatia, sends a number of personnel and equipment of the 101st Brigade of the National Guard of Croatia to the southern command of the Croatian army on temporary duty. These individuals are ordered to report to General Bobetko. In document 18, you will see a document of the 10th of June of 1992 in which Mr. Dario Kordic, from the Central Bosnian HVO regional headquarters, issues a permanent pass to an individual in Vares in Bosnia-Herzegovina giving free passage both through the Croatian community of Herceg-Bosna and the Republic of Croatia. Document 19 is another order from General Bobetko. This time the Croatian lieutenant-general issues an order that HVO, Croatian Defence Council military ID cards are to be issued to members of the HVO by June the 30th of 1992, and you will see that in paragraph 2.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: Please go a little bit more slowly, please. The interpreters are having a little problem following you and the Judges also. Go ahead, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: Within this order, he issues a direct order to the main headquarters of the HVO in Grude. Now, again, you will note that the printed heading on this document is Croatian community of Herceg-Bosna, Croatian Defence Council. Document 20. On the same day, General Bobetko issues orders to the operative group for southeast Herzegovina for operations in Bosnia-Herzegovina. These orders are issued from his Ploca forward headquarters in the Republic of Croatia. Both the HV and the HVO are being deployed by virtue of these orders. He orders deployment of HVO armour, tanks in the Stolac region, a coordinated military operation using both HV and HVO military assets in Bosnia-Herzegovina under the command of the Croatian general. Document 21. On the 15th of June of 1992, another order is issued in which units of the HVO and the HVO (sic) are deployed together by General Bobetko, and you will find a similar order of the 18th of June of 1992 in document 22. I have just noticed a mistake in the transcript where it's stated: "On the 15th of June of 1992, another order is issued in which units of the HVO and the HVO are deployed together." It should be "HVO and HV are deployed together." Move ahead now to document 23. This is a document of the 24th of July of 1992 in which, General then, Colonel Blaskic issues an order on behalf of the commander of the Central Bosnia OSHQ to send HVO troops to Croatia for training in reconnaissance missions. Document 24. On the 11th of September of 1992, the military post in Split, in the Republic of Croatia, confirms the delivery of a large quantity of ammunition to the HVO in Bugojno in Bosnia-Herzegovina. The receipt is signed by a colonel in the Croatian army. He signs the stamp of 4th Guards Brigade of the National Guard Corps of the Ministry of Defence for the Republic of Croatia. Document 25.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Please slow down.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: My apologies. I'll go deliberately slowly now. An order of the 19th of September, 1992, issued by Colonel Blaskic confirms that weapons and ammunition are moving from the Republic of Croatia to the HVO in Bosnia-Herzegovina and from the HVO in Bosnia-Herzegovina to the Republic of Croatia. Movement of military material from Bosnia-Herzegovina to the Republic of Croatia requires the signature of Mr. Dario Kordic or Colonel Blaskic. Document 26. On the 5th of October, 1992, Colonel Blaskic, as commander of the Central Bosnian operative zone, issues an order to commanders of his subordinate HVO municipal headquarters to provide to him the personal data of HV Croatian army officers in these HVO municipal headquarters. You will see in document 27 a document of the 6th of October of 1992. A similar order is issued by another HVO operative zone commander. This order makes it clear that Croatian army officers serving in the HVO cannot leave the HVO without a direct order from the Ministry of Defence in the Republic of Croatia. If we could now move into private session, because the next series of documents are confidential?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: Continue, Mr. Cayley.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President. (Private session)

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: (Open session)

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: The balance of the documents are all, I think, almost exclusively documents from the United Nations, and I'd like to draw your attention, Your Honours, to a number of these documents. Document 96 is a letter dated the 1st of February, 1994 from the Secretary-General addressed to the President of the Security Council. On page 1 of that letter, and I quote from the Secretary-General: "The Croatian army has directly supported the HVO in terms of manpower, equipment, and weapons for some time. Initially, the level of support was limited to individual and subunits, many of them volunteers. As the offensives of the Bosnia and Herzegovina Government forces against the HVO have become successful, the numbers of Croatian soldiers appear to have increased. It is assessed that in total there is the equivalent of three Croatian Brigades of regular Army personnel in Bosnia and Herzegovina, approximately 3.000 to 5.000 (this is an estimation, as it is impossible with UNPROFOR's assets to obtain required information for a more accurate account). There have been confirmed reports by UNPROFOR personnel that elements (troops and equipment) from the following Croatian Army (HV) units are indeed present in central and southern Bosnia and Herzegovina. 1 Guards Brigade; 2 Guards Brigade; 5 Guards Brigade; 7 Guards Brigade; 114 Brigade; 116 Brigade, 4th battalion; and Special military police."
