The report then goes on to explain the level of equipment being provided by the HV. On the same day that this letter is written, the permanent representative of the Republic of Croatia responds to the President of the Security Council, and he states, and this is document 97: "My Government does not deny that there are regular Croatian army troops in the border areas between the Republic of Croatia and the Republic of Bosnia and Herzegovina. They are stationed there in accordance with the Joint Agreement of 12 July, 1992 between my Government and the Government of the Republic of Bosnia and Herzegovina." Then in the final paragraph on that page, "My Government remains concerned about the welfare of ethnic Croat citizens of the Republic of Bosnia and Herzegovina which are under siege by the army of Bosnia and Herzegovina in the Vitez, Kiseljak, Usora, and Zepce enclaves and elsewhere." Document 99 is a letter from the permanent representative of Croatia enclosing a letter from Mate Granic, the Deputy Prime Minister of Croatia, a Minister for Foreign Affairs, and this letter is addressed to the Secretary-General of the United Nations. Mr. Granic says the following, and this is on page 3 in the pre-penultimate paragraph: "The Republic of Croatia is ready to call off the units of the Croatian Army on the left bank of the Neretva River and elements of the Croatian Army on the right bank of the Neretva." In the next paragraph he states: "Furthermore, as a measure aimed at easing the tensions in the area, the Government of the Republic of Croatia would advise the command of the Croatian Defence Council (HVO) to withdraw a part of its heavy weaponry in central Bosnia and to declare a cease-fire in the town of Mostar unilaterally." On the 17th of February, 1994, and this is document 100, the Secretary-General reverts to the Security Council, and he states the following, and this is on the final three paragraphs of page 2 of this document: "As of 17 February, UNPROFOR has not yet received any concrete proposals for a monitoring arrangement nor have any of the troop movements indicated in the above letter been observed. "In the absence of any observation of HV withdrawal movements beyond that on 10 February, UNPROFOR continues to assess that there still may be 5.000 HV troops in Bosnia and Herzegovina, although no HV command posts nor any full HV brigades operating as formed units have been identified. "It appears that HV troops are now being more circumspect and may be removing their HV insignia while in Bosnia and Herzegovina and replacing them with those of the HVO. UNPROFOR believes that HV insignia on a number of vehicles have been erased or repainted." Move ahead to document 102 where the permanent representative of Croatia to the United Nations addresses the Secretary-General and states in paragraph 2: "Croatian volunteers that had been situated in the Uskoplje-Rama area in Central Bosnia have returned to the Republic of Croatia on 10 February 1994. The convoy consisting of 44 vehicles with 12 heavy artillery weapons, 3 buses, and 650 volunteers crossed the Kamensko border-pass at 1700 hours and proceeded towards Split. "On 16 February at 1000, elements of the Croatian Army left the wider Neretva River region and have been repositioned in the Metkovic area on the territory of the Republic of Croatia. I have received information from my authorities that amongst the aforesaid elements of the Croatian Army were 600 soldiers, 4 battle tanks and 6 heavy artillery pieces." Document 106 is the actual cease-fire agreement between the Bosnian army forces and the HVO which is signed by the Chief of Staff, General Ante Roso, and the commander of the Bosnian army in Zagreb. Now, in this letter, and I don't intend to read it out, Mario Nobilo, who is the Permanent Representative of Croatia to the United Nations at this time, speaks of the possible presence of Croatian army units in Bosnia-Herzegovina. If we could now go back into private session for one or two final documents? (Private session)
